stage: HISTORIE (engine stage 6) - fractal axis + competing frames - cache
disputedNote: Even where this story begins is disputed - picking a start date is itself a position. Frames change emphasis and annotation, never the record.

frames.label: Jun 12 2026 IPO
frames.note: Under this frame the story begins on the Nasdaq debut day, when SpaceX shares opened and Musk's paper wealth crossed $1 trillion. The arc reads as a single market event with a clean before and after. This is the frame BBC, TASS and most market desks open with.

frames.label: 2002 SpaceX founding
frames.note: Under this frame the story begins when Musk founded SpaceX in 2002 with a reusable-rocket bet most investors called impossible. The IPO reads as the cash-out moment of a 24-year private build, not a sudden windfall. This is the frame NYT business coverage and the co-founder interview open with.

frames.label: 2008 NASA contracts
frames.note: Under this frame the story begins when NASA's COTS and CRS awards pulled SpaceX back from bankruptcy and seeded its launch monopoly. The trillion-dollar valuation reads as the compounding of two decades of public money and public risk. This is the frame Al Jazeera economy desks and policy critics open with.

frames.label: 2024 political turn
frames.note: Under this frame the story begins with Musk's hard-right political turn and racial-grievance posting in 2024-2025, which preceded the IPO payday. The trillionaire milestone reads as a reward earned during, not despite, that turn. This is the frame Mother Jones and left-leaning outlets open with.

bands.label: IPO and the first trillionaire
bands.summary: SpaceX debuted on Nasdaq on Jun 12 2026, raising about $75bn at a roughly $1.8tn valuation and tipping Musk's net worth past $1 trillion.

nodes.title: Pre-IPO critique frames listing as political reward
nodes.what: Two days before pricing, Mother Jones published a piece arguing the imminent trillionaire milestone came after Musk's 2024-2025 calls for a 'race war' and reframed the payday as a reward for that political turn. Market-desk previews running the same week described the listing in straight valuation terms.
nodes.disputed: Mother Jones describes the IPO as a reward for Musk's racial-grievance posting; market desks like Taipei Times and TASS describe it as the mechanical result of a listing priced at $1.8 trillion.

nodes.title: Bankers price SpaceX near $1.8 trillion ahead of debut
nodes.what: On the eve of trading, Al Jazeera reported SpaceX's IPO would value the company at about $1.8 trillion and quoted analysts warning the deal structure could be 'highly undesirable' for some shareholders. The BBC framed the same listing as Musk's biggest gamble yet, pointing to dual-class voting, lockups and concentration of control.

nodes.title: SpaceX debuts on Nasdaq, raises about $75bn
nodes.what: SpaceX shares began trading on Nasdaq on Jun 12 2026, with the offering raising about $75 billion at a valuation around $1.8 trillion. The listing completed a 24-year transition from privately held startup to public company and was covered live by BBC, Al Jazeera and Taipei Times. SpaceX co-founder Tom Mueller, identified as 'employee number one,' spoke to the BBC on debut day.

nodes.title: Musk's net worth crosses $1 trillion on paper
nodes.what: On the day of the listing, Musk's paper wealth tipped past $1 trillion, making him the first person publicly identified as a trillionaire. BBC, Al Jazeera, CGTN and TASS all reported the milestone within hours of the debut, citing his SpaceX stake combined with existing Tesla and xAI holdings. The New York Times ran a long retrospective the same day tracing the path from the 2002 founding to the Nasdaq bell.

nodes.title: Post-debut coverage confirms trillionaire status across outlets
nodes.what: The day after the listing, Taipei Times, CGTN and TASS reported that SpaceX's market capitalization held near $1.8 trillion after first-day trading, and that Musk's wealth crossing $1 trillion had been confirmed by multiple wealth trackers. Russian state agency TASS led with the milestone in its economy coverage.

nodes.title: Coverage shifts to what $1 trillion buys
nodes.what: Three days after the IPO, Al Jazeera published an interactive piece inviting readers to spend Musk's fortune, illustrating the scale of $1 trillion in personal wealth against national budgets and global aid figures. The piece marked the moment coverage moved from the market event itself to its cultural and political resonance.

bands.label: Pre-IPO political turn and roadshow
bands.summary: Musk's politics moved hard right while bankers prepared the listing and the press debated whether the IPO would be 'highly undesirable' for some shareholders.

nodes.title: Musk endorses Trump after Butler rally shooting
nodes.what: Within hours of the assassination attempt on Donald Trump at a Butler, Pennsylvania rally, Musk posted a full endorsement of Trump on X, his first formal presidential endorsement. He went on to fund the America PAC with reported contributions exceeding $250 million through Election Day, becoming the cycle's single largest individual donor.

nodes.title: Trump wins, Musk named to advisory role
nodes.what: After Trump's election victory, the president-elect announced Musk would co-lead a new Department of Government Efficiency advising on federal spending cuts and regulatory reform. Musk appeared regularly at Mar-a-Lago and on Air Force One during the transition.

nodes.title: Musk steps back from DOGE amid public rift
nodes.what: Musk's formal role as a special government employee wound down in late May 2025 after a public falling-out with Trump over the administration's tax-and-spending bill, which Musk attacked on X as fiscally reckless. The split prompted brief sell-offs in Tesla stock and renewed scrutiny of SpaceX's federal contracts.
nodes.disputed: Trump aides described the break as a personality clash driven by Musk's posts; Musk allies described it as a principled split over deficit spending.

nodes.title: SpaceX tender offer values company near $400bn
nodes.what: A secondary share sale led by existing investors valued SpaceX at roughly $400 billion, making it the most valuable private company in the world. The round was widely read by bankers as a dress rehearsal for a public listing, with Starlink revenue cited as the main driver.

nodes.title: SpaceX files S-1 with the SEC
nodes.what: SpaceX filed its registration statement for a public offering, disclosing Starlink subscriber counts, launch revenue and Musk's voting structure for the first time. The filing confirmed a dual-class share design preserving Musk's control after listing.

nodes.title: Roadshow opens in New York and London
nodes.what: SpaceX management began the formal investor roadshow in mid-May 2026, with stops in New York, London and the Gulf. Order books were reported as multiple times oversubscribed within the first week, and the offering size was lifted before pricing.

bands.label: Falcon, Starlink, Starship
bands.summary: Reusable Falcon 9 landings, the Starlink constellation buildout and Starship development pushed SpaceX's private valuation from billions into the hundreds of billions.

nodes.title: Dragon becomes the first commercial spacecraft to berth with the ISS
nodes.what: The COTS Demo 2 Dragon was captured by the International Space Station's robotic arm and berthed to the Harmony module. NASA used the flight to clear SpaceX for operational cargo runs under the Commercial Resupply Services contract.

nodes.title: Falcon 9 first stage lands back at Cape Canaveral
nodes.what: On the ORBCOMM OG2 mission, the Falcon 9 booster returned to Landing Zone 1 and touched down vertically after delivering its payload. It was the first time an orbital-class rocket first stage was recovered intact on land.

nodes.title: First operational batch of 60 Starlink satellites reaches orbit
nodes.what: A Falcon 9 from Cape Canaveral deployed the first 60 Starlink v0.9 satellites, beginning the buildout of the broadband megaconstellation. The launch opened a rapid cadence of Starlink missions that would put thousands of satellites in low Earth orbit over the following years.
nodes.disputed: SpaceX describes Starlink as bringing broadband to underserved regions; astronomers and the International Astronomical Union describe the constellation as a persistent source of optical and radio interference with ground-based observation.

nodes.title: Crew Dragon Demo-2 carries NASA astronauts to the ISS
nodes.what: Doug Hurley and Bob Behnken launched on a Falcon 9 from Kennedy Space Center's pad 39A and docked with the ISS the next day. It was the first crewed orbital launch from US soil since the Space Shuttle's retirement in 2011 and the first ever crewed flight by a private company.

nodes.title: Starship's first integrated flight test ends in mid-air breakup
nodes.what: The fully stacked Starship and Super Heavy booster lifted off from Starbase, Texas, lost several engines during ascent, failed to separate, and was destroyed by the flight termination system about four minutes in. The launch pad sustained heavy damage and the FAA grounded Starship pending a mishap investigation.
nodes.disputed: SpaceX described the flight as a successful test that cleared the tower and gathered data; FAA filings and environmental groups described it as a failed launch that scattered concrete debris over a wide area and triggered a formal mishap probe.

bands.label: NASA rescue
bands.summary: After three failed launches and near bankruptcy, NASA's COTS and CRS contracts gave SpaceX the cash and anchor customer that made the company viable.

nodes.title: Falcon 1 Flight 3 fails seconds after stage separation
nodes.what: SpaceX's third Falcon 1 attempt lifted off from Omelek Island carrying a small NASA technology demonstrator and two other payloads, then was lost when the spent first stage recontacted the second stage. It was the company's third consecutive failure and, by Musk's later account, left SpaceX with money for only one more attempt.

nodes.title: Falcon 1 Flight 4 reaches orbit
nodes.what: Six weeks after the third failure, Falcon 1 launched from Kwajalein with a mass simulator and became the first privately developed liquid-fueled rocket to reach Earth orbit. The success kept SpaceX alive long enough to close the NASA cargo contract still under negotiation that autumn.

nodes.title: NASA awards SpaceX a $1.6bn Commercial Resupply Services contract
nodes.what: NASA selected SpaceX and Orbital Sciences for the Commercial Resupply Services program, with SpaceX's share covering at least 12 cargo flights to the International Space Station using Falcon 9 and Dragon. The award came days before Musk has said the company would otherwise have run out of cash, and it became the anchor revenue stream behind every later SpaceX milestone.
nodes.disputed: Musk and SpaceX accounts describe the contract as a last-minute rescue that saved a near-bankrupt startup; NASA and several policy histories describe it as a competitive procurement won on price and technical merit under a program designed years earlier to seed commercial launch.

nodes.title: Falcon 1 Flight 5 delivers RazakSAT, SpaceX's first paying customer
nodes.what: Falcon 1 carried Malaysia's RazakSAT Earth observation satellite to low orbit from Kwajalein, marking the first commercial payload SpaceX put into space. The mission proved the company could fly for outside customers, after which SpaceX retired Falcon 1 to focus engineering on Falcon 9 and the NASA cargo manifest.

bands.label: Founding and Falcon 1
bands.summary: Musk founded SpaceX in 2002 with PayPal proceeds and a reusable-rocket thesis, surviving three Falcon 1 failures before reaching orbit in 2008.

nodes.title: Falcon 1 first launch fails
nodes.what: SpaceX's first Falcon 1 lifted off from Omelek Island in the Marshall Islands and failed about 33 seconds into flight after a fuel leak triggered an engine fire. The vehicle and its DARPA FalconSat-2 payload were lost. SpaceX traced the cause to a corroded aluminum nut and pressed on toward a second attempt.

nodes.title: NASA picks SpaceX for COTS
nodes.what: NASA announced that SpaceX and Rocketplane Kistler would share roughly $500m in funded Space Act Agreements under the Commercial Orbital Transportation Services program, with SpaceX's share around $278m to develop the Falcon 9 rocket and Dragon capsule. The award gave the still pre-orbital company a government anchor for cargo flights to the International Space Station. Kistler was later dropped and replaced by Orbital Sciences.

nodes.title: Falcon 1 second flight reaches space but not orbit
nodes.what: The second Falcon 1 launched from Omelek with a demonstration payload and successfully separated stages, but the upper stage began to roll during its burn and shut down early at about 289 kilometers altitude. The rocket reached space but did not reach orbital velocity. SpaceX called the flight a partial success and used the data to redesign propellant slosh baffles and control software.
nodes.disputed: SpaceX described the mission as a major step that validated stage separation and most of the vehicle; outside analysts and trade press described it as a second failure that left the company two-for-two on missed orbits with cash running low.
